questions.stem: Which condition turns an alkene into an alkane by adding hydrogen?

options.explanation: Hydrogen adds across the double bond on the nickel surface.
UV initiates radical substitution in alkanes, not hydrogenation.
Acid catalysts accompany steam addition, not hydrogen gas.
Steam brings in OH groups, not plain hydrogen.

questions.stem: What does the addition of bromine water to an alkene produce?

options.explanation: Bromine atoms stay attached; the product is halogenated.
Both bromine atoms settle, one on each alkene carbon.
One bromine only would leave the second atom unaccounted.
Alcohols come from steam addition, not bromine.

questions.stem: Which reagent set adds to an alkene to give an alcohol?

options.explanation: Bromine adds bromine atoms, not hydroxyl groups.
That reagent substitutes on halogenoalkanes; alkenes need the acid-catalysed steam route.
Water adds as H-OH across the double bond.
That pair yields the plain alkane.

questions.stem: What product forms when hydrogen bromide adds to ethene?

options.explanation: That needs Br2, not HBr.
That needs steam plus the acid catalyst.
That needs H2 over nickel - the bromine must appear somewhere.
H takes one carbon, Br the other.

questions.stem: Why do alkenes undergo addition rather than substitution with most reagents?

options.text: The electron-rich pi bond attracts attacking species that open it
options.explanation: The exposed density invites reagents to split across the bond.
The double bond IS the functional group.
Saturation describes alkanes and resists addition, not alkenes.
The alkane neighbour's behaviour does not dictate alkene reactions.

questions.stem: List the four addition reagents named in the specification and the product class each delivers.
questions.modelAnswer: Hydrogen over nickel gives an alkane; halogens give a di-substituted halogenoalkane; hydrogen halides give a mono-substituted halogenoalkane; steam with an acid catalyst gives an alcohol.

questions.stem: State the equation for the hydrogenation of ethene, naming the catalyst.
questions.modelAnswer: CH2=CH2 + H2 -> CH3CH3, with the nickel catalyst written over the arrow.

questions.stem: Explain why hydrogenation requires a catalyst while the reaction with bromine does not.
questions.modelAnswer: Hydrogen molecules are tightly held and unreactive toward the pi bond until the nickel surface splits them into reactive atoms, whereas bromine already polarises itself beside the electron-rich double bond and needs no surface help.

questions.stem: Propene reacts in turn with hydrogen over nickel and then with steam over an acid catalyst. Name the organic product of each step.
questions.modelAnswer: Hydrogenation first converts propene to propane; steam addition then cannot proceed on the saturated propane, so the sequence shows why the addition order matters - only the alkene step delivers the alcohol, via direct hydration of propene to propan-2-ol if performed before hydrogenation.

questions.stem: What does cold, dilute, acidified potassium manganate(VII) add across an alkene's double bond?

options.explanation: Hydrogenation is the nickel-catalysed route.

options.text: One hydroxyl group to each alkene carbon, giving a diol
options.explanation: Two -OH units arrive, one per double-bond carbon.
Both carbons are serviced - the product is a diol, not a mono-ol.
Bromine belongs to the halogen addition, not oxidation.

questions.stem: What observation signals that an alkene has oxidised with manganate(VII)?

options.explanation: No precipitate marks this oxidation.

options.text: The solution turns purple from colourless
options.explanation: The change runs the other way.
The reagent is consumed and reduced, losing its colour.
Orange describes bromine water, not manganate(VII).

questions.stem: Which product results from oxidising ethene with acidified manganate(VII)?

options.explanation: A single OH would make the mono-ol - a second carbon is still hungry.
Oxidation adds oxygen; hydrogenation gives ethane.
Full cleavage chemistry is beyond this specification's scope.
One OH lands on each of the two carbons.

questions.stem: Why is the manganate(VII) test for C=C bonds also called an oxidation rather than an addition?

options.text: The manganate species is reduced while delivering oxygen to the alkene
options.explanation: Electron bookkeeping runs from manganate to the alkene carbons.
The alkene gains OH groups; nothing is lost.
Two new C-O bonds clearly form.

options.text: The purple colour is the oxidation
options.explanation: The colour change evidences the redox; it is not itself the process.

questions.stem: Which statement pairs the reagent with its correct use?

options.explanation: Steam makes alcohols; the saturation test uses bromine.

options.text: Acidified KMnO4 - detects and oxidises C=C bonds
options.explanation: One reagent, both roles.
Bromine adds bromine; hydrogen needs the nickel route.
Nickel belongs to hydrogenation.

questions.stem: State the conditions and the organic product for the manganate(VII) oxidation of propene.
questions.modelAnswer: Cold, dilute, acidified potassium manganate(VII) adds two OH groups across the double bond to give propane-1,2-diol.

questions.stem: Describe the colour change in the manganate(VII) oxidation of any alkene.
questions.modelAnswer: The purple manganate(VII) solution decolourises as the oxidant is reduced while oxidising the alkene's double bond.

questions.stem: Explain why the manganate(VII) result confirms an unsaturated bond as convincingly as the bromine result.
questions.modelAnswer: Both reagents survive unchanged against saturated hydrocarbons but are consumed by a C=C bond - one bleaches from orange, the other from purple - so a colour loss under either reagent evidences a reactive double bond.

questions.stem: Cyclohexene is shaken with cold acidified manganate(VII). Name the organic product and the observation.
questions.modelAnswer: The ring's double bond opens to cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol, and the purple reagent decolourises as it oxidises the alkene.
